title: This Totally Free App Can Free Up Space on Your Mac
gist: Wired recommends Purge, a free open-source macOS cleanup app with no ads or upsells. Its notable feature removes Apple Intelligence's offline models (10+ GB) and blocks reinstallation, which matters because Apple removed the toggle to disable those models in macOS 27.

insights.claim: Apple removed the toggle in macOS 27 that let users disable its preloaded offline Apple Intelligence models altogether.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Apple is pushing on-device AI as non-optional, a sign of how central it is to the platform strategy and a possible source of user pushback.
insights.quote: Apple removed the toggle in macOS 27 that lets you disable them altogether

insights.claim: Apple Intelligence's offline models in macOS 27 can take up more than 10 GB of local storage.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: On-device AI uses a lot of storage, which pushes buyers toward higher-capacity (higher-margin) Mac configurations.

insights.claim: The offline models power features such as notification summaries, writing suggestions and the new AI-powered Siri.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Shows which user-facing features depend on local models, and so what users lose if they strip them out.

insights.claim: Purge can delete the Apple Intelligence models and prevent macOS from reinstalling them, a workaround for Apple's removal of the opt-out.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Third-party tools that undo platform AI defaults show there is demand to opt out of bundled AI.
insights.quote: Purge will delete the models and prevent macOS from reinstalling them

insights.claim: Most Mac disk-cleanup apps are sold on subscription, while Purge is free, open source, and has no ads or upsells.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Free open-source tools weaken the subscription model for paid Mac utility apps.
insights.quote: There are no ads or upsells

insights.claim: Purge works from lists of files known to be safe to delete and a list it never touches, and it moves files to the Trash instead of deleting them permanently.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Safety-first design is how a cleanup tool earns trust without a brand behind it.

insights.claim: Deleting an app in Finder leaves its settings, caches and downloaded files behind; in the author's case, leftover data from deleted apps came to several gigabytes.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Points to a long-standing macOS storage-management gap that third-party apps fill.
